chapter_title: Design of Micropiles for Soil Slope Stabilization

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Micropiles stabilize slopes by one of two approaches. Approach 1: battered micropiles through the unstable slope to below the potential slip surface, fixed at the surface to a concrete cap beam, each resisting by axial, shear and bending resistance (Figure 6-1). Approach 2: many more, closely spaced micropiles forming a coherent micropile-soil structure that acts like a gravity wall (Figure 6-2). The chapter gives a step-by-step method for Approach 1 (Table 6-1); Approach 2 concepts are in Appendix A.
sections.body: (pp. 6-1 to 6-3) In addition to structural foundation support, micropiles are used for structural slope stabilization, designed to provide the required restraining forces by one of two approaches. Approach 1: battered micropiles are installed through the unstable slope to a specific depth below the potential slip surface and affixed at the ground surface to a concrete cap beam (Figure 6-1); the individual micropiles provide resisting forces through the mobilization of axial, shear and bending resistance. Their spacing along the slope is evaluated from the number of micropiles needed (per lineal meter) to provide the minimum required stabilizing force, typically the force required to raise the slope to a prescribed minimum factor of safety. Approach 2: micropiles are installed similarly, but many more are used (Figure 6-2), close enough to create a coherent structure of micropiles and soil that behaves much like a gravity retaining wall, the restraining force coming from sliding resistance along the bottom of the micropile group; individual micropiles carry relatively small loads, and the group inscribes and internally reinforces the soil mass so it acts as a unit. The chapter presents a step-by-step design method for Approach 1 (Table 6-1), and Section 6.9 presents three case histories using Approach 1. A step-by-step method for Approach 2 cannot be developed at this time, since limited data are available to confirm a design method and the system has limited applicability in current US practice; design concepts for Approach 2 groups are in Appendix A.

sections.title: Step 1: Identify Project Specific Constraints and Evaluate Micropile Feasibility
sections.summary: Micropile slope stabilization is usually considered for remote sites or difficult access. Seven common constraints are listed. Micropiles compete with ground anchors, soil nail walls, driven piles and drilled shafts; they need a small work area, are buried and install in virtually any ground. First-order cost: $4,000 to $11,000 per lineal meter of slope. They are likely cost-effective only with a structure near mid-height of the slope, and the method requires a single well-defined slip surface (Figure 6-3).
sections.body: (pp. 6-3 to 6-6) Slope stabilization projects in which micropiles may be feasible are usually in remote areas or where difficult site access is a concern. Other common constraints: (1) space restrictions (limited ROW, on-site storage for materials, access for equipment, restrictions on traffic disruption); (2) interference with above-ground utilities and nearby structures; (3) working on an unstable slope (controlled cut/fill, excess seepage around the work area, soil or rock fall hazards); (4) environmental concerns (noise, vibration, transport of material, protection of animals and plants); (5) landscape aesthetics such as scars from access road cuts or excavations; (6) disposal of excavated rock or soil; and (7) cost. Micropiles will most often be compared with ground anchors, soil nail walls, or driven piles or drilled shafts. They have come into favor because construction is relatively simple, needs a small work area and suits limited equipment access (landslides in hilly, steep or mountainous areas), though a specialty geotechnical contractor is still required. Other advantages: reduced excavation compared with earth retaining systems (built top-down), improved aesthetics (the system is completely buried) and installation in virtually any ground type, important where an upper competent layer (colluvium or talus, difficult for driven piles or drilled shafts) overlies soft, wet soil resting on rock. Cost-effectiveness depends on the forces required: long landslides or deep slip surfaces may need restraining forces too large for micropiles, although battering mobilizes axial restraint, and in some cases additional restraint, usually ground anchors, is required. For first-order comparisons, micropiles for slope stabilization cost $4,000 to $11,000 per lineal meter of slope ($1,200 to $3,400 per lineal ft), the high end for long micropiles (more than 15 m (50 ft) to reach the top of the slide surface), low production (less than 90 m (300 ft) per day) and much rock drilling. Previous designs and contractor experience indicate micropiles will likely be cost-effective only if unbalanced slope forces can be resisted by a micropile structure at approximately mid-height of the slope; to limit movements of a roadway near the top of the slope a single structure would likely not suffice, since the slope could be unstable in front of it, and multiple structures may not be cost effective. The design method assumes the micropiles below the potential slip surface 'tie' the slope mass above to the more competent ground below (they serve as dowels) and that deformations concentrate at the slip surface, so maximum bending moments and shears occur near it. Instrumentation data on slope movements must be reviewed: the method requires movements at a well-defined critical potential slip surface, e.g., concentrated lateral movement at about 8 m (25 ft) depth at a landslide in Summit County, Ohio (Figure 6-3). Where movements are less localized or more than one potential slip surface may exist, other measures such as anchored walls should be considered.

sections.title: Step 2: Identify Performance Requirements
sections.summary: The primary requirement is that the stabilized slope meet or exceed a target factor of safety for static and seismic stability: typically 1.3 to 1.5 static (depending, e.g., on whether other structures are supported by the slope and on how limited the geotechnical data are) and 1.1 for pseudo-static seismic analysis. Other requirements: corrosion protection, permissible groundwater variation during construction, maximum test loads and allowable steel and concrete stresses. Slope design is not codified in AASHTO (2002).
sections.body: (pp. 6-6 to 6-7) The primary performance requirement for a slope stabilization project is for the stabilized slope to meet or exceed a target slope stability factor of safety with respect to static and seismic slope stability. Typical static factors of safety range from 1.3 to 1.5 depending on, for example, whether other structures are supported by the slope and whether only limited geotechnical data are available. For seismic slope stability analyses (based on pseudo-static analysis), a target value of 1.1 is typically used. Other performance (and/or design) requirements include: a prescribed level of corrosion protection for the micropiles; permissible variation in groundwater levels during construction; maximum loads that can be carried (as part of load testing); and allowable stresses for steel and concrete. Design of earth slopes (and stabilization of slopes) is not codified in, for example, AASHTO (2002); design criteria for slopes are typically developed on a project-specific basis.

sections.title: Step 3: Review Available Information and Geotechnical Data
sections.summary: Exploration and testing (Mayne et al., 2001; GEC No. 5, Sabatini et al., 2002) should establish: topography (survey if maps are old or the site was modified); lateral extent of the landslide; subsurface profile and groundwater, with borings into the competent material below the slip surface; pore pressures, including possible cutoff by the micropiles; soil and rock parameters (correlations from index data for preliminary design only); the critical slip surface, also needed for laterally loaded pile analyses; and site seismicity (pseudo-static analysis).
sections.body: (pp. 6-7 to 6-9) Existing slope conditions should be assessed by review of available information and a focused subsurface exploration and laboratory testing program (guidance: Manual on Subsurface Investigations, Mayne et al., 2001; GEC No. 5 'Evaluation of Soil and Rock Properties', Sabatini et al., 2002). The program should obtain: Topography of the area, used to develop cross sections for slope stability analysis; if recent maps are not available or site topography has been modified since the last survey, a ground surface survey should be performed, since accurate slope geometry is critical. Lateral extent of the landslide or potential landslide area, from site inspection and aerial photographs; usually multiple parallel cross sections are analyzed with 2-dimensional limit equilibrium methods to find the slip surface with the minimum factor of safety, and that cross section is used for design. Subsurface profile and groundwater conditions at the critical cross section from historical and new borings; for micropile-stabilized slopes, borings should be advanced into the competent materials below the potential slip surface that will serve as the micropile resistance zone. Groundwater from boring logs, piezometers and observation wells is used to model pore pressures; slope movements are often related to large precipitation events, and where back analysis is required, pore pressures at the time of instability must be developed. Design groundwater levels should consider the effect of the micropile structure; spacing is typically large enough that pore pressure buildup from a hydraulic cutoff effect is insignificant, but where close spacing or significant recharge is possible, the Owner should require seepage analyses considering spacing, installation methods (e.g., grout travel), precipitation and hydraulic conductivity; subsurface drainage may be required or the system designed for long-term seepage pressures. The importance of an accurate assessment of pore pressure conditions cannot be overemphasized. Soil and rock parameters (unit weights and shear strength) are needed for slope stability and for the structural capacity of micropiles (p-y analyses); where undisturbed sampling is difficult or impossible, collect index data (Atterberg limits, grain size, moisture content) and use correlations (GEC No. 5), primarily for preliminary design and not as a substitute for a comprehensive investigation. Critical slip surface: from inclinometer data where the slope has moved, boring logs and stratigraphy; it is often at the interface just above a competent soil or rock surface where water may be perched; it is also required for laterally loaded pile analyses, as the location of maximum lateral micropile movement. Site seismicity: seismically induced destabilizing forces are typically evaluated by pseudo-static slope stability analysis (Kavazanjian et al., 1997).

sections.title: Step 4: Evaluate Factor of Safety of Existing Slope
sections.summary: Slope stability analyses give the minimum factor of safety (FSmin) and the critical slip surface for static and seismic cases. A slope that has failed is by definition at FS = 1.0 and is back-analyzed: (i) estimate trial strengths (residual, c' = 0 and phi'r from Figure 6-4, Stark and Eid, 1994); (ii) analyze several cross sections with conditions at the time of failure; (iii) adjust parameters until FS = 1.00, with a critical surface consistent with the field. Otherwise analyze circular and planar surfaces.
sections.body: (pp. 6-9 to 6-11) Using the information from Step 3, slope stability analyses evaluate the factor of safety of the slope to be stabilized, presumably about 1.0 (if the slope has undergone significant movements) or slightly higher. The minimum factor of safety (FSmin) and the location of the critical potential slip surface are evaluated, for the static and seismic cases, and compared with the target minimum factor of safety. A special case is a slope known to have failed or undergone significant downslope movement, which by definition is at FS = 1.0 at the time of failure; micropiles for slope stabilization have been used most commonly for such failures (landslides). Shear strength for this case is adjusted by back-analysis: i. Estimate analysis parameters. If the slope has moved sufficiently, the residual drained friction angle may be used (e.g., c' = 0, phi' = phi'r) for the material where movements occurred; Figure 6-4 relates phi'r of clayey landslide material to liquid limit and clay fraction (for example, clay content between 25 and 45 percent and liquid limit 60 give a residual friction angle of 18 degrees). These are the trial strengths (phi trial and c trial); parameters of the other materials are evaluated from available information and usually not adjusted. ii. Perform slope stability analysis for several cross sections with the best available pore pressures, shear strength, stratigraphy and topography at the time of failure; the failure surface location needs to be known with some certainty. iii. Adjust parameters until FS = 1.00. Shear strength is only one unknown; pore pressures and the critical surface at the time of failure, and their uncertainty, should also be considered. A back analysis that gives FS = 1.00 with a critical surface inconsistent with the field should not be relied upon. Where the existing slope has FS above 1.0 but below the target, shear strengths and groundwater are evaluated as in Design Step 3, the critical surface is estimated from available data, FSmin is evaluated with circular and planar slip surfaces, and stratigraphy is used to check the calculated slip surface.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: At this stage the existing slope has been shown to be unstable or marginally stable, with a factor of safety below the target. The geotechnical and structural design of micropiles for slopes is outside typical practice for most geotechnical engineers, so 6.6 gives background on load transfer mechanisms and analysis methods for Design Steps 5 through 13; the complete design is demonstrated in Section 6.7.
sections.body: (pp. 6-11 to 6-12) At this stage in the design process, an existing slope has been shown to be either unstable or marginally stable, with a calculated slope stability factor of safety less than a target value. The remaining steps comprise designing a micropile system to improve or otherwise stabilize the slope. The steps specific to the geotechnical and structural design of micropiles used for slopes are outside the typical design practice for most geotechnical engineers; for this reason, this section provides background information on load transfer mechanisms and analysis methods used for Design Steps 5 through 13. The complete design of a micropile stabilized slope is demonstrated in Section 6.7.

sections.title: Evaluating the Additional Force Required to Obtain Target Factor of Safety
sections.summary: Micropiles must provide the force required to raise the slope's factor of safety from its existing value to the target value (Hreq). Slope stability programs determine Hreq in three stages: (1) choose a location for the micropiles; (2) model the micropiles explicitly to find the required restraining force; (3) check the stability of the slope away from the micropile.
sections.body: (p. 6-12) Micropiles used for slopes are designed to prevent downward movement of the slope mass above the potential slip surface and must be capable of providing the force required to stabilize the slope, i.e., the force required to increase the factor of safety of the slope from an existing value to a target value. Slope stability analysis programs are used to determine this additional force (Hreq). The analyses are performed in three stages: (1) a location is chosen for the micropiles; (2) the micropiles are modeled explicitly in the slope stability analysis to determine the required restraining force; and (3) the stability of the slope away from the micropile is evaluated by additional slope stability analysis.
key_points: Hreq: force required to raise the slope's factor of safety from the existing value to the target value

sections.title: Micropile Location Within Slope Cross Section
sections.summary: Hreq varies with the micropile's location in the slope. In an example slope (Figure 6-5), a single micropile was moved across the section and its shear force increased until FSmin = 1.3 (Figure 6-6). Near the toe or the crest no force could reach the target (Figures 6-7 and 6-8): the most critical slip surface passes upslope or downslope of the micropile. The maximum benefit was for a structure near the middle of the slope.
sections.body: (pp. 6-12 to 6-16) The magnitude of Hreq varies with the location of the micropile within the slope, as demonstrated with the example slope geometry in Figure 6-5. Several analyses were performed with a single micropile at different locations in the cross section; at each location the shear force provided by the micropile was increased until a target factor of safety (FSmin) of 1.3 was achieved for the slope. The results (Figure 6-6) indicate that, for this example, a micropile structure at or near the toe or at or near the crest of the slope would be ineffective: regardless of the force the micropiles could develop, the target factor of safety (FSmin = 1.3) could never be achieved (see Figures 6-7 and 6-8 for the most critical slip surface). The maximum benefit from micropiles corresponds to a micropile structure placed in the vicinity of the middle of the slope.

sections.title: Methods to Model Resisting Force from a Micropile
sections.summary: Although the structure will have battered upslope and downslope legs joined by a cap beam (Figure 6-9), it is modeled as a single vertical micropile from the cap beam into a competent layer (Figure 6-10). Approach 1: Hreq as a large cohesive strength in a thin (say 0.5 m) slice where the micropile crosses the slip surface (Figure 6-11: Hreq = c x L = c x w / cos alpha). Approach 2: input the restraining force directly where software allows. Vary c or the force until the target factor of safety is reached.
sections.body: (pp. 6-16 to 6-18) While micropile structures for slope stabilization typically include a battered upslope 'leg' and a battered downslope 'leg' connected at the ground surface by a concrete beam (Figure 6-9), the structure is modeled as a single vertical micropile from the ground surface (at the design cap beam location) to a sufficient depth into a competent layer (Figure 6-10). The shear capacity, inclination and number of micropiles required to resist Hreq are evaluated in subsequent design steps. The slope stability input files from Design Step 4 are typically modified in one of two ways. Approach 1: the shear resistance provided by the single vertical micropile, Hreq, is modeled as a relatively large cohesive shear strength assigned to the soil layer where the micropile crosses the potential slip surface; with a width of, say, 0.5 m, the program develops a single 0.5-m slice with that strength. The relationship between Hreq and cohesive strength is shown in Figure 6-11; Hreq is oriented at the same angle as the bottom of the slice. Repeat the analyses, changing the cohesive strength until the factor of safety equals the target value. Approach 2: some slope stability software packages accept a micropile restraining force directly at any location, so a thin layer of large cohesive strength is not needed; repeat the analyses, changing the restraining force until the factor of safety equals the target value.

sections.title: Evaluating Slope Stability Away From Micropile
sections.summary: Slip surfaces entirely upslope or entirely downslope of the micropile may have factors of safety below the target, so they are searched separately with the micropile ignored (Figure 6-12). The method does not allow for losing the soil in front of the micropiles: excavation there (Figure 6-13) could cause excessive deflection or structural failure. The Owner can require calculations of the maximum excavation in front (recommended regardless), or fence off and sign the area.
sections.body: (pp. 6-19 to 6-21) The previous analysis gives the location and the required restraining force for the target factor of safety, but slip surfaces away from the micropile may have factors of safety below the target, so additional analyses should be performed in which the micropile is ignored, with search limits set for slip surfaces entirely upslope and entirely downslope of the micropile (Figure 6-12). Downslope stability raises practical issues (Figure 6-13): a roadway at the toe could later be widened by excavation at the toe, or excavation may be part of long-term maintenance. Many earth retaining structures conservatively neglect passive resistance in front of the wall; for micropiles, the assumption of zero passive soil resistance in front of the micropile is not considered in the design method presented. If slope material in front of the micropile moved away through instability or were removed in maintenance, the structure would likely experience excessive deflection or structural failure of the downslope micropiles from loss of lateral support. Two approaches address this: as part of the design submittal the Owner can require calculations establishing the maximum excavation in front of the micropiles that keeps a minimum factor of safety and keeps the soil in front stable to support the front row (recommended to be performed and provided to the Owner regardless of whether the Contract Documents request it); or the Owner may fence off the area and post signs that excavation should not be performed.

sections.title: Load Transfer in Micropiles
sections.summary: Micropiles resist by grout-to-ground axial resistance above and below the slip surface plus shear and bending; maximum lateral movement and maximum axial force occur near the slip surface (Figure 6-14). Battering adds axial tension (upslope leg) or compression (downslope leg). The ultimate side resistance above the slip surface (Eq. 6-1) must be resisted below it with FS = 2.0 (Eq. 6-2, Figure 6-15). Load testing is recommended (Chapter 7).
sections.body: (pp. 6-21 to 6-24) Micropiles resist unstable slope forces through axial resistance at the grout-to-ground interface both above and below the potential slip surface plus structural (shear and bending) resistance. The maximum lateral micropile movement is assumed to occur near the elevation of the critical potential slip surface, a reasonable assumption since micropiles are relatively flexible; Figure 6-14 shows axial force and bending moment diagrams for the legs at Littleville, Alabama (Brown and Chancellor, 1997). The capacity of individual micropiles can be increased significantly by battering them relative to the slip surface: slope movement then tends to pull the micropile away from the slip surface (axial tension) or push it towards it (axial compression), mobilized as side resistance at the grout-to-ground interface. For micropile structures without ground anchors, the upslope leg will typically be in tension and the downslope leg in compression. The maximum axial force occurs near the critical slip surface, similar to soil nails. The micropile must be embedded sufficiently below the slip surface to prevent pullout (tension) or failure by insufficient bearing capacity (compression): the side resistance below the slip surface must resist the axial forces developed above it (Figure 6-15). That axial force is assumed equal to the ultimate side resistance that could develop above the failure surface, Pult (Eq. 6-1), with alpha_bond-above the grout-to-ground ultimate bond strength above the critical slip surface (Table 5-3), Labove the length from the slip surface to the bottom of the cap beam and d the micropile diameter. Micropiles also develop flexural resistance; the objective is a system with enough structural capacity to resist the unbalanced slope force (Hreq) without structural failure in combined axial loading and bending. The required length below the slip surface, Lbelow, is given by Eq. 6-2, with alpha_bond-below from Table 5-3 and FS = 2.0. Load testing of slope stabilization micropiles is not commonplace and required side resistance has relied on contractor experience in similar ground; this document recommends load testing (Chapter 7).

sections.summary: Bending moment and shear capacity of a single vertical micropile are treated under 6.6.4.1 (bending moment capacity) and 6.6.4.2 (shear capacity); no text is printed under this heading.

sections.title: Evaluation of Bending Moment Capacity of Single Vertical Micropile
sections.summary: The shear resistance of a micropile is the maximum shear force that makes the maximum bending moment just equal to the ultimate bending moment Mult. Mult is evaluated with LPILE (2005) or another laterally loaded pile program, for P = 0 and for P = Pult (Eq. 6-1), since moment capacity varies with axial load. Where ground anchors may reverse axial loads, check P = Pult in both compression and tension and design for the lower Mult.
sections.body: (p. 6-25) The shear resistance of a micropile corresponds to the maximum shear force that can be applied to the micropile that results in a maximum bending moment within the micropile (at any location) just equal to the ultimate bending moment of the micropile. To evaluate it, the ultimate bending moment (Mult) of the single micropile is checked; it can be conveniently evaluated with the computer program LPILE (2005) or other soil-structure interaction programs for laterally loaded piles and shafts. Because micropiles are battered, they develop axial resistance through side friction between the grout and the ground, and since the bending moment capacity varies with the applied axial load, Mult is checked for two limiting axial load conditions: (1) P = 0; and (2) P = Pult (Eq. 6-1). The shear capacity corresponding to the ultimate bending moment is used (rationale in Section 6.8). Axial loads may be tension or compression: in general the uphill micropile is in tension and the downhill micropile in compression, but where ground anchors are incorporated the direction may change with anchor stressing and lock-off loads. Mult should therefore be evaluated for P = Pult applied in compression and in tension, and the design based on the case giving the lower Mult, and therefore the lower available shear resistance.
key_points: Shear resistance = the shear force at which the maximum bending moment in the micropile just reaches Mult

Check Mult for two axial loads: P = 0 and P = Pult (Eq. 6-1)

sections.title: Evaluation of Shear Capacity of Single Vertical Micropile
sections.summary: The shear capacity is the shear at the slip surface that makes the maximum moment equal Mult. It is found by separate laterally loaded pile analyses of the micropile above (up) and below (down) the slip surface with shifted p-y curves (Figures 6-16, 6-17), for P = 0 and then P = Pult. Criteria: same axial load and shear; boundary moments equal and opposite; same head slope at the slip surface; free head. Example (Figure 6-18): M = 87 kN-m matched slopes, Mmax = 161 kN-m = Mult.
sections.body: (pp. 6-25 to 6-29) The maximum shear force the micropile can carry is the shear force applied at the elevation of the slip surface that gives a calculated maximum bending moment equal to Mult; it depends on the stiffness (p-y response) of the ground above and below the slip surface and on the flexural rigidity of the micropile, and can be evaluated with laterally loaded pile analyses such as LPILE. The portion above the potential slip surface (the 'up' analysis) and the portion below (the 'down' analysis) are analyzed separately; for the up analysis the previously determined p-y curves are relocated relative to the top of the pile in the analysis (Figure 6-16 shows p-y curves for the entire length; Figure 6-17 shows the adjustment for the up and down analyses). The up and down analyses are performed as a set, first for minimum axial resistance (P = 0) and then for maximum axial resistance (P = Pult). The boundary shear forces and moments at the slip surface are internal forces, so the results must satisfy: the same axial load in both analyses; the same input shear force magnitude and direction at the slip surface; input bending moments equal in magnitude and opposite in sign; the same calculated slope of the micropile head at the slip surface; and the micropile head modeled as free. Figure 6-18 shows the iteration: for Analysis 1 a slip surface moment of 40 kN-m gave unequal slopes (a discontinuity, not possible); for Analysis 2 a moment of 87 kN-m gave equal head slopes, with a maximum moment of 161 kN-m below the slip surface, approximately equal to the ultimate bending moment of the section, so the analysis is complete. The procedure is demonstrated in Section 6.7.6.

sections.title: Shear Capacity of Battered Micropile Group
sections.summary: Hult of an inclined micropile at the slip surface combines its shear Q and axial force P (Figure 6-19): H = Q cos psi + P sin psi (Eq. 6-5), psi measured from the normal to the slip surface (Figure 6-21). Following Poulos and Davis (1980), Pult develops at about 30 degrees: Hult = QP=0 for psi up to 10 degrees, QP=Pult cos psi + Pult sin psi for psi of 30 or more, interpolated between (Eqs. 6-6 to 6-9, Figure 6-20). The pair capacity is the sum for the two legs (Eq. 6-10).
sections.body: (pp. 6-30 to 6-33) This step evaluates the maximum lateral force (Hult) that an inclined (battered) single micropile can resist at the critical slip surface, including the effect of a non-horizontal slip surface; the value compared with Hreq is the sum of the Hult values of each battered micropile in the cross section. The assumed forces are shown in Figure 6-19 for a vertical micropile (axial resistance zero, P = 0) and an inclined micropile (axial resistance equal to the ultimate axial resistance from the ground above the slip surface, P = Pult); the inclination angle psi may be defined as the angle between the slip surface and the vertical axis of the pile. Summing the shear (Q) and axial (P) forces in the x and y directions gives Eqs. 6-3 and 6-4, which solved simultaneously give the lateral pile load along the slip surface (Eq. 6-5), coincident with the orientation of Hreq (Figure 6-11). Ultimate values of P and Q are used: the minimum axial resistance is zero and the maximum is assumed equal to Pult. According to Poulos and Davis (1980), Pult may be assumed to develop in a pile inclined at approximately 30 degrees, giving Eq. 6-6 (psi = 0) and Eq. 6-7 (psi of 30 degrees or more). Although axial resistance should be mobilized even at very small inclinations, it is conservative to assume it is not mobilized until a nominal inclination is reached, and relying on it at small angles implies a certainty in the slip surface angle that probably cannot be achieved by subsurface investigation. Therefore, for inclinations between 0 and 30 degrees: Hult = QP=0 for 0 < psi <= 10 degrees (Eq. 6-8), and Hult is interpolated for 10 < psi < 30 degrees (Eq. 6-9; Figure 6-20 shows the relationship for a specific micropile design, but Eqs. 6-7 to 6-9 can be used directly; see the example in Section 6.7.7). The inclination angle psi is the angle between the axis perpendicular to the slip surface and the micropile axis, or between the axis perpendicular to the micropile axis and the slip surface (Figure 6-21); solutions for positive and negative angles are identical for Eqs. 6-3 and 6-4 (Poulos and Davis, 1980), so psi is written as positive in Eq. 6-5 regardless of sign. The angle is assessed where each of the two micropiles crosses the slip surface, and the combined capacity of the upslope and downslope micropile is given by Eq. 6-10.

sections.title: Spacing Required to Provide Required Force to Stabilize the Slope
sections.summary: The resisting force of the micropiles per unit length of cap beam must at least equal Hreq (Design Step 5), and the distance between individual micropiles along the cap beam (Soffset) must permit construction (Figure 6-22). With the leg capacities from Eq. 6-5 and the pair capacity from Eq. 6-10, the maximum spacing between two upslope (or two downslope) micropiles is Smax = Hult-pair / Hreq (Eq. 6-11).
sections.body: (pp. 6-33 to 6-35) Figure 6-22 shows a typical micropile layout at the cap beam. The resisting force provided by the micropiles per unit length of cap beam must be at least equal to Hreq (from the slope stability analysis in Design Step 5), and the distance between individual micropiles along the cap beam (Soffset) must be large enough to permit ease of construction. The shear capacities of the battered upslope micropile (Hult(psi_us)) and battered downslope micropile (Hult(psi_ds)) are evaluated using Eq. 6-5 and their combined capacity (Hult-pair) using Eq. 6-10; Smax, the spacing between two upslope or two downslope micropiles (Figure 6-22), is then evaluated by Eq. 6-11.

Eq. 6-11: Smax = Hult-pair / Hreq, with leg capacities from Eq. 6-5 and pair capacity from Eq. 6-10

sections.title: Potential for Soil Flow Between Micropiles
sections.summary: If micropiles are too far apart or the soil above the slip surface is very weak, soil may move between them (plastic flow, Figure 6-23). The lateral force per unit thickness q follows Ito and Matsui (1975) as given by Hassiotis et al. (1997) (Eq. 6-12). Integrated from the slip surface to the cap beam it gives Hult-soil/pile. If Hult-soil/pile is less than Hult-pair/2, reduce Smax and repeat; the design spacing must satisfy Hult-soil/pile >= Hult-pair/2.
sections.body: (pp. 6-35 to 6-37) If micropiles are spaced too far apart and/or the soil above the slip surface is very weak, soil may move between adjacent micropiles (Figure 6-23), a failure mechanism termed plastic flow. Ito and Matsui (1975) developed a theory to evaluate plastic flow between piles; the lateral force per unit thickness of soil acting on the micropile, q, is calculated by Eq. 6-12 (Hassiotis et al., 1997), where c = cohesion of the soil, phi = friction angle of soil, gamma = unit weight of soil, z = depth from ground surface, D1 = Smax (Eq. 6-11) and D2 = opening between micropiles (Figure 6-23: D2 = D1 - b, b = micropile diameter). The ultimate horizontal force on the micropile from soil moving between adjacent micropiles, Hult-soil/pile, is q integrated over the length of the micropile from the slip surface to the cap beam (spreadsheet example in Section 6.7.9). Hult-soil/pile is compared with the average resistance of the upslope and downslope pair (Hult-pair/2): if the plastic flow conditions are satisfied, Smax from Eq. 6-11 need not be reduced; if Hult-soil/pile < Hult-pair/2, plastic flow governs, Smax should be reduced and the plastic flow analysis repeated for the new spacing. The final design spacing is the spacing that satisfies Hult-soil/pile >= Hult-pair/2.

sections.title: Design Example for Slope Stabilization with Micropiles
sections.summary: The example stabilizes an embankment that creeps, particularly in rainy periods (Figure 6-24): roadway surcharge 12 kPa; right-of-way rules out a berm; micropiles assumed the best solution. Silty clay (unit weight 21.2 kN/m3, liquid limit 60, up to 30 percent clay size) overlies calcareous siltstone (23.0 kN/m3; phi = 23 degrees, cohesion intercept 480 kPa). The critical slip surface came from a crest scarp, toe heave and preliminary analyses.
sections.body: (pp. 6-37 to 6-39) This section provides a complete design example for micropiles used for slope stabilization. The problem is stabilizing an embankment that exhibits creep movements, particularly during rainy periods; the cross section and subsurface information are shown in Figure 6-24. The roadway surcharge for design is 12 kPa; right-of-way limitations preclude a berm, and micropiles are assumed to have been determined to be the best solution. The slope consists of silty clay overlying calcareous siltstone. From laboratory tests, the unit weight of the silty clay is estimated at 21.2 kN/m3 (134.9 pcf) and of the calcareous siltstone at 23.0 kN/m3 (146.4 pcf). The silty clay has a liquid limit of 60 and hydrometer results indicate up to 30 percent clay size material. Shear strength tests on the bedrock indicate a friction angle of 23 degrees with a cohesion intercept of 480 kPa (69.65 psi). The critical slip surface was identified from surficial features (scarp at the embankment crest and heaving near the toe) and from preliminary slope stability analyses.

sections.title: Step 4: Evaluate Factor of Safety of Existing Slope
sections.summary: The slope had moved, so its existing factor of safety was taken as 1.0 and the silty clay was back-analyzed with SLIDE (Spencer's method). Trial strengths: phi'r = 18 degrees (Figure 6-4, LL = 60, 30 percent clay) and c = 25 kPa from experience gave FS = 1.67 (Figure 6-25). Eqs. 6-13 and 6-14 give phi' = 11 degrees and c' = 15 kPa, with FS = 1.0 and a slip surface consistent with the field (Figure 6-26). Use with caution; nonzero c' tends to reduce with deformation.
sections.body: (pp. 6-39 to 6-41) Slope stability analysis computes the minimum factor of safety of the slope (FSmin), with programs such as XSTABL or SLIDE and methods such as Simplified Janbu, Simplified Bishop or Spencer. Because the slope had previously moved, its existing factor of safety was assumed to be 1.0 and the silty clay shear strength corresponding to FS = 1.0 was back-analyzed. i. Estimate shear strength parameters: since the slope has moved sufficiently, the residual drained friction angle can be used (phi' = phi'r) as the trial strength; Figure 6-4 with LL = 60 and a clay fraction of 30 percent gives phi'r = 18 degrees (phi trial), and the cohesion was assumed to be 25 kPa (3.63 psi) (c trial) from previous experience with these materials. Analyses with SLIDE and Spencer's limit equilibrium method gave FS = 1.67 for the trial strengths (Figure 6-25). The trial parameters were modified using Eqs. 6-13 and 6-14, giving phi' (modified) = 11 degrees and c' (modified) = 15 kPa (2.18 psi). This back-analysis method should be used with caution: the calculated critical failure surface must be compared with the observed one, and a nonzero effective stress cohesion intercept should be used with caution since deformations tend to reduce it. With the modified parameters the computed FS = 1.0 (Figure 6-26) and the critical slip surface was reasonably consistent with the actual slip surface in the field.

sections.title: Step 5: Evaluate Additional Force Required To Obtain Target Factor of Safety
sections.summary: With a target factor of safety of 1.3 and the micropile modeled near midslope in SLIDE (2004), the strength assigned to the micropile was varied until the target was reached (Figure 6-27): Hreq = 650 kN/m (44.54 k/ft) of slope length. Slip surfaces entirely upslope and downslope gave FSup = 1.30 and FSdown = 1.35 (Figure 6-28), not less than the target, so the location is appropriate; otherwise move it or add a micropile.
sections.body: (pp. 6-41 to 6-43) A target factor of safety (FStarget) of 1.3 was selected and the micropile was modeled using Approach 2 (see Section 6.6.2.2) with the computer program SLIDE (2004). Several analyses were performed with the micropile at approximately a midslope location, and the shear strength assigned to the micropile was varied until the target factor of safety was achieved (Figure 6-27). The additional force required from the micropile (Hreq) is 650 kN/m (44.54 k/ft) of slope length. Additional analyses confirmed acceptable factors of safety for slip surfaces upslope and downslope of the micropile (Figure 6-28): FSup = 1.30 and FSdown = 1.35, so the location is deemed appropriate. Had the factor of safety of the slope entirely downslope or entirely upslope of the micropile been less than FStarget, the location would need to be changed or an additional micropile would be required.

sections.title: Step 6: Select Micropile Cross Section
sections.summary: A Type A micropile with API-N80 casing (177.8 mm OD, 11.50 mm wall, Fy = 552,000 kPa) in grout (f'c = 27.6 MPa) in a drill hole of at least 0.229 m is used (Figure 6-29). The ground is considered nonaggressive, so no reduction of casing thickness is required.
sections.body: (pp. 6-43 to 6-44) The micropile cross section is selected as shown in Figure 6-29: a Type A micropile with API-N80 casing, outside diameter 177.8 mm, wall thickness 11.50 mm, Fy = 552,000 kPa, grout f'c = 27.6 MPa, drill hole 0.229 m minimum. The ground is considered nonaggressive and no reduction in steel casing thickness is required.

sections.title: Step 7: Estimate Length Of Micropile
sections.summary: Ltotal = Labove + Lbelow (Eq. 6-15). Labove is about 10 m (Figures 6-24, 6-27). Eq. 6-1 gives Pult = 66 kPa x 10 m x pi x 0.229 m = 475 kN (stiff silts and clays, Table 5-3). Eq. 6-2 with 515 kPa (hard shale, Table 5-3; siltstone is closer to shale) and FS = 2.0 gives Lbelow = 2.6 m. Preliminary LPILE runs showed 2.6 m did not give fixity, so Lbelow was increased to 4.5 m (15 ft).
sections.body: (pp. 6-44 to 6-45) The total length of the micropile is Ltotal = Labove + Lbelow (Eq. 6-15), where Labove is the length between the ground surface and the critical slip surface and Lbelow the length below the critical slip surface. In the example, Labove is approximately 10 m (printed '(3.28 ft)'), approximated from Figure 6-24 at the micropile location in Figure 6-27. sections.body: (pp. 6-45 to 6-47) The ultimate bending moment, Mult, of a single vertical micropile with the cross section in Figure 6-29 is evaluated with LPILE (model in Figure 6-30). Besides the section geometry, the analysis needs (1) grout compressive strength, (2) yield strength of the steel casing and (3) modulus of elasticity of the steel. sections.title: Step 9: Evaluate Shear Capacity of Single Vertical Micropile
sections.summary: p-y curves from the Mult runs at depths above and below each layer change (Figure 6-31) are relocated for up (10 m) and down (4.5 m) analyses (Figures 6-33, 6-17). sections.body: (pp. 6-47 to 6-51) The maximum shear capacity of a single vertical micropile (Q) is found iteratively by laterally loaded pile analyses. p-y curves may be generated within LPILE in the same analyses used for Mult, at various depths and specifically just below and above each transition between soil or rock layers (Figure 6-30); the depths chosen are shown in Figure 6-31. The capacity is calculated using (1) Mult from the P = 0 case and (2) Mult from the P = Pult case, with up and down analyses (process in Figure 6-32), for P = 0 first and then P = Pult. As printed: 1. Set up the up and down analyses with the micropile section, material properties, soil or rock parameters for each layer and p-y curves relocated relative to the slip surface (Figure 6-17). 2. Input a trial shear force Q (same magnitude and sign in both analyses) and a trial internal moment M (same magnitude, negative for the up and positive for the down analysis); the trial values are arbitrary, but if the initial Q exceeds the Q that ultimately corresponds to Mult the solution will not converge (head slopes diverge with each iteration). 3. Run both analyses and compare the head slopes; if unequal, change M and re-run; when equal, note Mmax from each analysis. 4. Compare Mmax (greater of the up and down values) with Mult for the corresponding axial load. 5. If Mmax is approximately equal to Mult, Q is determined; otherwise change Q and re-run. 6. Repeat for P = Pult, using its Mult. (The printed steps refer to M as set 'in Step 1', Q 'in Step 5', and repeating 'steps 1 through 4', comparing in 'step 3'.) Output is in Appendix B. The up analysis uses a pile length of 10 m (32.8 ft) and the down analysis 4.5 m (15 ft); p-y values determined at 10 m depth are assigned to 0 m in the up analysis (Figures 6-33, 6-17a). For P = 0, QP=0 = 365 kN (82 k) with Mmax = 161.3 kN-m (119.0 k-ft), equal to Mult (Table 6-2); for P = Pult, QP=Pult = 330 kN (74.2 k) with Mmax = 147.7 kN-m (108.9 k-ft), equal to Mult. Both are used in the next steps.

sections.title: Step 13: Perform Structural Design of Concrete Cap Beam
sections.summary: The steel-reinforced CIP cap beam spans and anchors the micropiles at the surface, typically 2 m wide and 1 m deep, with at least two to three micropile diameters of embedment for fixity; design follows AASHTO (2002) Section 8. Consider anchor reactions, load transfer from fixity (soil-structure analysis for shallow slide planes) and differential settlement stresses. Example summary: 177.8-mm casing 4.5 m into bedrock, legs at 3 and 21 degrees, spacing at most 1.25 m, test loads 950 kN and 760 kN.
sections.body: (pp. 6-54 to 6-57) The steel-reinforced CIP concrete cap beam spans and anchors the micropile array at the ground surface. It is typically 2 m wide and 1 m deep, but in general should have sufficient height and width to allow at least two to three micropile diameters of embedment to promote fixity of the upslope and downslope micropiles. Structural design follows typical reinforced concrete methods (Section 8 of AASHTO (2002)). Specific considerations: where ground anchors are used, the cap beam provides their reaction for stressing and lock-off and must be designed for these forces; where anchors are not incorporated, axial loads transferred towards the surface should be small (particularly for a deep slide plane), but fixity of the group at the cap beam causes load transfer to the beam, and where the slide plane is relatively shallow, cap beam moments may be on the order of those at the slide plane, so soil-structure interaction analyses should be performed; relatively significant deflections may need consideration, since anchor stressing, non-uniform depth to competent material and/or compression of soil within the unstable mass may cause differential settlement along the beam, and the resulting bending and torsional stresses should be considered. Summary of the design example: Type A gravity-grouted micropiles of API-N80 casing (OD 177.8 mm) embedded 4.5 m (15 ft) into bedrock; upslope leg battered 3 degrees and downslope leg 21 degrees, the micropiles of each pair as close together as construction permits; spacing between two upslope and two downslope micropiles no more than 1.25 m; all micropiles connected at the surface by a concrete beam; verification load tests of micropiles with a 4.5-m (15-ft) bond length in rock to 950 kN (213 kips), i.e., 2.0 x the calculated axial resistance above the slip surface, and proof tests to 760 kN (printed '(171 kN)'), i.e., 1.6 x that resistance (Chapter 7).

sections.title: Shear Capacity of Micropiles for Analysis
sections.summary: A failed slope is at FS = 1.0 with loads and resistances known and equal; micropile shear is added to the resisting forces (not as a negative driving force) until the target, e.g., 1.3, is reached. In allowable stress terms the service load on the micropiles is zero, unlike a retaining wall; the ultimate shear is assumed mobilized at failure, as in reinforced slope design, without allowable-stress reductions (only corrosion loss). Conservatism can be added through properties, phreatic surface, target FS or maximum shear.
sections.body: (pp. 6-58 to 6-59) The shear load an individual micropile provides is assumed to correspond to the maximum shear force in the micropile when it has reached its ultimate bending capacity. Rationale: a slope that has failed (movement observed, possibly stopped, or continuous or intermittent movement measured) has a factor of safety equal to 1.0; since the design is predicated on good knowledge of the failure surface and the pore pressures at the time of failure, the loads and soil resistances are reasonably well known and equal in magnitude. The slope must now be stabilized to a target factor of safety (e.g., FS = 1.3): using the back-analyzed strengths, a micropile shear force is added until the target is calculated, and it is recommended that this force be added to the resisting forces (or moments) in the limit equilibrium calculations rather than treated as a negative driving force or moment. In an allowable stress design format, the service loads on the micropile are zero, since the slope is 'stable' at FS = 1.0; for a retaining wall, by contrast, the service loads at FS = 1.0 are not zero and may be full active earth pressure. Micropiles are added to increase the factor of safety, assuming that if their ultimate shear capacity were mobilized at a limit (failure) state the factor of safety would be 1.3. This is exactly consistent with reinforced slope design, where the design strength of the reinforcement at a specific design life, Tal, is used and slope stability analyses verify the target factor of safety; as there, no reduction to an allowable stress is used, but whereas reinforcement strength is reduced for creep, durability and construction damage, micropile strength may be reduced for potential steel loss from corrosion. Additional conservatism may be prudent where the failure surface and/or residual strength are not well understood or the soil may continue to creep, through soil properties, phreatic surface assumptions, the target factor of safety, the maximum micropile shear force, or a combination; probabilistic analysis (Duncan et al., 1999) can show the effect of ranges of material parameters.
key_points: Micropile shear used in design = maximum shear when the micropile reaches its ultimate bending capacity
A failed slope is at FS = 1.0 with known, equal loads and resistances (failure surface and pore pressures well known)
Add micropile shear to the resisting forces or moments, not as a negative driving force, until the target (e.g., 1.3) is reached
In allowable stress terms the micropile service load is zero at FS = 1.0, unlike a retaining wall under active pressure
Ultimate shear assumed mobilized at failure, consistent with reinforced slope design (Tal); no allowable-stress reduction, but allow for corrosion loss
Add conservatism through soil properties, phreatic surface, target FS or maximum micropile shear where uncertain
Probabilistic analysis (Duncan et al., 1999) can show the effect of parameter ranges
sections.applicability: Why the micropile shear used in design is the shear at its ultimate bending capacity, and where conservatism can be added.

sections.title: Stabilization of Blue Trail Landslide Using Micropiles, Wyoming
sections.summary: US 26/89 beside the Snake River canyon (Figure 6-38) had moved since construction in 1955-1960; target FS 1.3. Micropiles beat regrading with a toe berm, a bridge and drilled shafts on cost, variable ground and access. Two micropile walls and an MSE wall were designed (Figure 6-39), a third wall added; ground anchors were enlarged after a higher seismic coefficient. Micropiles were battered 30 degrees, 19-34 m long (Figure 6-40); 478 micropiles and 40 anchors. Measured loads: Table 6-4.
sections.body: (pp. 6-59 to 6-62) The Blue Trail Landslide project is on U.S. Highway 26/89 between Alpine Junction and Hoback Junction, Wyoming, next to the canyon of the Snake River (Figure 6-38). The highway, built between 1955 and 1960, had experienced episodes of movement from the landslide. Alternatives reviewed to stabilize the slide to a desired factor of safety of 1.3 included regrading with a toe berm, a bridge over the entire slide, and drilled shafts near the toe (Hasenkamp, 1999); they were not cost effective. Micropiles were selected because they were less expensive and could be built in highly variable ground under restricted access, with traffic maintained and minimal environmental impact. The design followed the approach in this chapter. Originally two micropile walls (two sets of upslope and downslope micropiles) and an MSE wall were designed (Figure 6-39): the upper wall 3 m below the roadway and the lower wall between the road and the toe of the slide; a third wall was later added along the western edge about 12 m (39 ft) below the roadway. The original design had a single ground anchor at each wall location; early in construction the restraining force of the lower wall had to be increased significantly because a reviewing agency required a much higher seismic coefficient, which was done by significantly increasing the capacity of its ground anchors. Micropiles were battered 30 degrees from vertical and were 19 to 34 m (62 to 112 ft) long; ground anchors were installed at 30 degrees from horizontal (Figure 6-40). It was the first Wyoming project using micropiles and ground anchors for permanent landslide stabilization. Instrumentation: slope inclinometers, survey monuments, tilt plates, strain gauges on micropile casings, load cells on four anchors and piezometers, recording wall and slope movement, load transfer to micropiles and anchors, and pore pressures. Micropile walls were installed before the anchors, the lower wall first, the upper second and the middle last; 478 micropiles and 40 ground anchors were installed. Instrumentation showed movements were significantly reduced. Measured axial loads were less than assumed in design, and measured maximum moments were about 8 to 80 percent (average 30 percent) of the ultimate moment capacity of the steel pipe (Table 6-4), so performance was acceptable. In the lower wall, axial loads and moments were opposite to the design assumption because of large anchor lock-off loads; upper-wall micropiles were in compression in both directions, most likely from the surcharge of the MSE wall and roadway over the upper insert wall.

sections.title: Stabilization of Sum-271 Landslide Using Micropiles, Ohio
sections.summary: I-271 northbound in Richfield Township, Summit County, Ohio: about 21 m of valley fill over thin weak normally consolidated lacustrine soils on strong overconsolidated lacustrine soils; movement caused pavement settlement and cracking. ODOT chose micropiles over regrading with toe berms (Liang, 2000); ground anchors were added. The wall had 154 Type A micropiles, 1.2-1.8 m apart, battered 30 degrees, and 41 anchors 3.5 m apart (Figure 6-41). Maximum axial force near the slip surface; moments near zero there.
sections.body: (pp. 6-62 to 6-65) The SUM-271 project is on Interstate 271 northbound in Richfield Township, Summit County, Ohio. About 21 m (70 ft) of valley fill overlies relatively thin, weak layers of normally consolidated fine-grained lacustrine soils with strong overconsolidated lacustrine soils beneath; slope movements caused pavement settlement and cracking. The alternatives were regrading with toe buttress berms or micropiles (Liang, 2000), and the Ohio Department of Transportation (ODOT) selected micropiles. The design followed the approach in this chapter; because micropiles could not completely develop the required resisting forces, ground anchors were added. The wall consisted of 154 Type A micropiles spaced 1.2 to 1.8 m (4 to 6 ft) apart and battered 30 degrees from vertical, and 41 ground anchors spaced 3.5 m (12 ft) apart and battered 30 degrees from horizontal (Figure 6-41). Inclinometers, strain gauges on the micropiles (axial loads and moments throughout construction) and high-capacity load cells on the anchors showed that the NRM wall and anchors arrested the slope movement. Detailed finite element analyses (Liang, 2000) simulated the construction stages (earthwork, pile cap, drilling and installation of micropiles, anchor stressing) and were compared with the monitoring data. Conclusions: 1. The maximum axial force in each micropile occurred near the slip surface (about 30 ft below the ground surface) (Figure 6-42), with directions and magnitudes consistent with the construction stages: the upslope micropile was initially in tension; after anchor tensioning a portion near its top remained in tension and the rest of the wall was in compression; compression in the downslope micropile was reduced by anchor tensioning, but no tension developed in it. 2. Bending moments were near zero where the maximum axial forces occurred (Figure 6-43); changes through construction were small, primarily due to the small stiffness of the micropiles, and the maximum moments were reasonably predicted by the finite element analyses.

sections.title: Stabilization of Littleville Landslide using Micropiles, Alabama
sections.summary: US Route 43: fill of sandstone and shale over shale weathered at the top (the failure surface); slides since the 1950s road, worse after 1970s widening, until a micropile wall with ground anchors was built in 1997 (Brown and Chancellor, 1997). 114-mm casing (8-mm wall), 7 m long, battered 30 degrees; 432 micropiles and 44 anchors (Figure 6-44). Over two years movement ceased; axial forces about half the estimated ultimate; FS about 1.3; maximum moments 5 to 9 percent of capacity.
sections.body: (pp. 6-66 to 6-67) The Littleville landslide is on a section of US Route 43, Alabama, in fill of sandstone and shale cut from adjacent hillsides over shale weathered along its top surface, believed to be the failure surface. Soon after the 1950s highway was built the road surface dropped from slides in the fill; holes were filled and the road repaved; in the 1970s the roadway was widened and the slope flattened, but rainy periods brought more failures, and creep continued until a micropile wall with additional stabilization by ground anchors was built in 1997 (Brown and Chancellor, 1997). The design followed the approach in this chapter (typical section, Figure 6-44). The micropiles had 114-mm (4.5 in.) diameter steel casing with an 8-mm wall, design lengths of 7 m (23 ft), battered 30 degrees from vertical; 432 micropiles and 44 ground anchors were installed. Instrumentation over two years recorded slope movement (inclinometers), pore pressures and stresses in the micropiles and anchors. Water levels were relatively stable, fluctuating about two or three feet. Slope movement had effectively ceased, without approaching failure in the micropiles: mobilized axial forces were below the estimated ultimate axial load by a factor of about two, and the factor of safety was calculated to be about 1.3 as originally estimated. Upslope battered micropiles were in tension near the slide plane and downslope micropiles in compression; higher moments developed near the slide surface, with measured maximum moments about 5 to 9 percent of the ultimate moment capacity. Anchor loads decreased slightly over time, attributed to small movements in the uphill direction.
